title: From One Slope to Every Slope

steps.body:
In precalculus you squeezed the secant onto the tangent and got **one number**: the slope of f at one point.

Now do it at every x at once. Each input has its own slope, and a rule that hands one output to each input is a **function**.

That function is the derivative, f′.
Drag x. The tangent turns above; f′ draws itself below.

widget.prompt: f(x) = x². Drag x until the tangent has slope 6 — and watch what you are drawing underneath.
widget.successFeedback: x = 3, slope 6. Now look at the curve you traced below: it came out a straight line through the origin, f′(x) = 2x. You did not compute that — you DREW it, one tangent at a time. The derivative is a function, and that is the whole shift.
widget.lowFeedback: The tangent is shallower than 6 (or tipping downhill). Slide right: on x² the slope climbs steadily with x.
widget.highFeedback: The tangent is steeper than 6. Slide back left — the slope IS 2x, so it passes 6 exactly once.

predict.prompt: On y = x², you need the tangent slope to read 6. Starting from x = -3, you'll find it…

options.label: To the right of where you start
To the left of where you start
In two places — either direction works

predict.reveal: On x² the slope at x is 2x — it climbs steadily left to right, so slope 6 lives at exactly one spot: x = 3. One slope, one place; that's what makes 2x a function of x.

cml.actionGoal: Move along a function and coordinate position, local slope, and derivative graph.

explanationVariants: The tangents you traced had slopes −4, 0 and 4 at x = −2, 0 and 2 — which is 2x every time. So f′(x) = 2x.
f′ is not a number attached to a point; it is a rule attached to the whole curve, and here that rule is 'double the input'.

widget.prompt: You traced f′ for f(x) = x². What kind of object is f′?

options.label: A function — one slope for each input, here f′(x) = 2x.
options.feedback: Right. That is the promotion: from a slope AT a point to a slope FUNCTION over the whole domain.

options.label: A number — the slope of the curve.
options.feedback: A curve has no single slope; it has a different one at every point. That is precisely why the derivative must be a function.

options.label: The tangent line at a point.
options.feedback: The tangent is a LINE at one x. f′ is the rule that tells you the slope of that line for every x at once.

options.label: The limit of a single secant.
options.feedback: That is f′ at ONE point — the precalculus version. Doing it at every point is what turns it into a function.

steps.body: Use the definition once, by hand.
explanationVariants: f(x+h) − f(x) = (x+h)² − x² = 2xh + h². Divide by h to get 2x + h, and let h → 0: f′(x) = 2x.
The h that survives division is exactly the h that dies in the limit — which is why the answer is clean.

widget.prompt: f(x) = x². Simplify [f(x+h) − f(x)]/h before taking the limit.

options.label: 2x + h
options.feedback: Right — and now h → 0 kills the leftover h, leaving f′(x) = 2x. The division by h is legal precisely because h is not yet zero.

options.label: 2x
options.feedback: That is the answer AFTER the limit. Before it, the h² term leaves a stray h behind: 2x + h.

options.label: 2x + h²
options.feedback: The h² was divided by h, so it comes down to h, not h². Expand carefully: (2xh + h²)/h = 2x + h.
That is what you get if you substitute h = 0 too early — the same 0/0 trap you met in limits. The cancellation must happen first.

steps.body:
Three notations, one object:

**f′(x)** — Lagrange. Compact; good for stating rules.
**dy/dx** — Leibniz. It *looks* like a fraction, and in the chain rule it behaves like one.
**d/dx[ ]** — the operator. Read it as "differentiate what follows".

They are the same function wearing different clothes.

explanationVariants: f′(3) = 6 and f(3) = 9, so the tangent is y − 9 = 6(x − 3), i.e. y = 6x − 9.
A line needs a point and a slope. The curve gives the point; the derivative gives the slope.

widget.prompt: f(x) = x², so f′(x) = 2x. Find the y-intercept of the tangent line at x = 3.

commonErrors.feedback: That is f(3), the y-value where the tangent touches the curve — not where it crosses the axis. Run the line back to x = 0: y = 9 + 6(0 − 3) = −9.
That is the slope f′(3), not the intercept. Use it in y − 9 = 6(x − 3) and set x = 0.
The tangent at (3, 9) with slope 6 is nowhere near the origin. y = 6x − 9 crosses at −9.

widget.fallbackFeedback: y − 9 = 6(x − 3) → y = 6x − 9, so the intercept is −9.

steps.body: Read a slope off a graph you cannot see.
hints: You are told f′, the SLOPE function. Feed it the x you care about.
f′(x) = 2x means the slope at x = −4 is 2(−4).
A negative slope means the curve is falling there — and the size says how steeply.
explanationVariants: f′(−4) = 2(−4) = −8. The curve is falling steeply at x = −4, even though f(−4) = 16 is positive and large.
Height and slope are independent facts. f can be high while f′ is negative — that is a curve on its way down from a great height.

commonErrors.feedback: That is f(−4), the HEIGHT of the curve. The derivative reports the SLOPE, which is 2(−4) = −8. A curve can be high and falling at the same time.
The sign is wrong. f′(x) = 2x, and 2 × (−4) is −8: on the left arm of the parabola the curve is going DOWN.
That is x itself. The rule doubles it: f′(−4) = 2(−4) = −8.

widget.fallbackFeedback: f′(x) = 2x, so f′(−4) = −8 — the curve is falling steeply there.

takeaways: The derivative is a FUNCTION: one slope for every input, not one number for one point.
f′(x) = lim(h→0) [f(x+h) − f(x)]/h — and the cancellation must happen before h reaches 0.
f′ hands you the tangent line for free: the curve gives the point, the derivative gives the slope.
steps.teaser: Next: read f′ straight off the shape of f — and meet a flat tangent that is not a peak.

concept.body: f tells you **how high**. f′ tells you **how steep**. They are different questions about the same point, and their answers are unrelated: a curve can be high and falling, or low and climbing.

explanationVariants: f(2) = 4 is the height. f′(2) = 2(2) = 4 is the slope. They happen to agree here, and that is a coincidence of x = 2.
Ask which question you are being asked: how high, or how steep?

widget.prompt: f(x) = x² and f′(x) = 2x. Find the SLOPE of the curve at x = 5.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the height f(5). The slope is f′(5) = 2(5) = 10.
That is x. Double it: f′(5) = 10.
